body:
The Federal Reserve announced a rate hike on Wednesday, pushing the private equity industry—already mired in exit difficulties—into even more dangerous territory. A record $349 billion is trapped in "zombie funds" that have exceeded their ten-year lifespans without exiting investments, while roughly $500 billion sits in funds in their seventh to tenth year facing overrun risk. The industry entered the year hopeful that rate cuts would spark a dealmaking recovery; that expectation has now been completely shattered, and shares of major alternative asset managers fell in response.

The rate hike's impact on private equity is multidimensional. Floating-rate loan costs for portfolio companies climb in tandem with benchmark rates, and potential buyers—facing elevated financing costs—are unwilling to pay the valuations PE firms need to complete exits, making deals increasingly difficult to close. At the same time, software investments are facing additional pressure from AI-driven disruption, and private credit businesses are also grappling with valuation turbulence. Shares of major alternative asset managers including Apollo Global Management (APO), Blackstone (BX), and KKR (KKR) have fallen notably this month as rate-hike expectations intensified.

The private equity business model is built on completing a "buy—improve—exit" cycle within roughly ten years: fund managers raise capital from institutional investors such as pensions and insurers using their own capital as a foundation, acquire companies while layering on leveraged loans borne by the acquired businesses themselves, and ultimately sell for a profit, repay loans, collect management fees, and return gains to investors.

Rising rates directly undermine this logic chain. According to PitchBook data, assets trapped in zombie funds—funds that have exceeded their ten-year lifespans with investments still unexited—surged approximately 65% from the end of 2021 to the end of 2025, with investors' capital awaiting return reaching a record $349 billion. After the Fed's 2022 rate hikes, sales of PE-held companies had already slowed substantially; this latest round of hikes will push even more funds into zombie territory.

Mitchell Mansfield, managing director at Kroll, said of the trend: "You're going to see more funds enter zombie status. The longer these funds persist, the more investor capital returns tend to stagnate, and then decline."

Exit bottlenecks are directly transmitting to the fundraising side. According to PitchBook data, as of September 11, the industry has raised $211.9 billion this year, on track for its worst performance since at least 2020. Full-year 2025 fundraising totaled $334.4 billion, down from $376.9 billion the prior year—a clear downward trend.

Institutional investors are tightening commitments. Angela Rodell, former CEO of the Alaska Permanent Fund and now a senior advisor at Star Mountain Capital, said that going forward, investors "will only renew with specific relationships they have confidence in, and more private equity funds will shut down as a result."

Persistently weakening returns are compounding the predicament. The average private equity fund return in 2025 was roughly 7%, the weakest since 2011, even as the U.S. economy maintained robust growth over the same period. Declining returns make it harder for pensions, insurers, and endowments to meet funding targets, while capital locked in funds that cannot be withdrawn and redeployed further constrains institutional investors' room to maneuver.

Apollo co-president Scott Kleinman said bluntly on a Monday conference call: "I do think the number of managers will decline, and some managers that expanded rapidly over the past decade will have to shrink." He added that Apollo continues to attract investors because its recent fund returns have outperformed the industry average.

Beyond rate hikes, the private equity industry faces another structural pressure: the past decade's aggressive bets on software companies made in a low-rate environment are now colliding with AI-driven disruption. According to PitchBook data, private equity allocates on average roughly 14% of capital to software companies, with a large share of deals concentrated in the 2020–2021 period when rates were at rock bottom.

As the loans backing these acquisitions mature, defaults are expected to spike next year and in 2028. Thoma Bravo has already lost $5 billion this year on customer-service software company Medallia—which defaulted and was taken over by lenders. Thoma Bravo is currently negotiating loan extensions with debt investors for its other software companies, including cybersecurity firm Sophos.

Clearlake Capital is under similar pressure. The Santa Monica, California-based firm leveraged its technology investing expertise to grow assets under management from roughly $8 billion in 2017 to $185 billion, but some software investments have hit headwinds.

According to regulatory filings from private credit funds, lenders have marked down valuations on a $2.1 billion loan to HR software company Cornerstone OnDemand and a roughly $1.5 billion loan to healthcare software company Symplr Software by more than 30% each. Clearlake is negotiating resolutions with holders of both loans.

Anant Kumar, portfolio manager at Benefit Street Partners, noted: "Over the long term, if high rates persist, these companies will face greater cash pressure and default with higher frequency."

Private credit—the other core business of private equity managers—is likewise unable to escape this round of rate-hike shock. Persistently rising rates will plunge the private credit market into turmoil, further eroding managers' overall revenue streams.

Private equity funds now control more than $2 trillion in assets in the United States, and the stress they are under is transmitting to the broader financial system, affecting pensions and insurers that depend on PE fund exit proceeds.

Sara Werner, partner at law firm Lowenstein Sandler, said: "It's absurd to say the golden age of private equity will never return, because markets are cyclical—but the question is how long these funds can wait for the valuations they want."

Analysts believe the spiral of compression—expanding zombie fund scale, rising fundraising difficulty, declining management fee income, and accelerating industry consolidation—is becoming increasingly clear as rates head higher once again.
